specPoints.text: understand how division of a cell by meiosis produces four cells, each with half the number of chromosomes, and that this results in the formation of genetically different haploid gametes

primer.text: Sex cells need half a chromosome set each, and building them takes two divisions. This note walks meiosis from chromosome doubling through both splits to four genetically different haploid daughters, then sets the comparison table beside mitosis so you can quote the differences the examiner asks for.

lessons.title: Two Divisions, Four Different Daughters
lessons.opening: Meiosis is the division that builds gametes: the chromosomes double first, two rounds of division follow, and four daughter cells emerge, each carrying half the starting number and each genetically distinct from its siblings.
keyPoints: Meiosis is a nuclear division producing cells that are genetically different.
Chromosomes double before the divisions, as they do before mitosis.
The first division separates chromosome pairs; the second separates the copies.
Four haploid daughter cells result, each with one chromosome of each pair.
Halving matters because fertilisation would otherwise double the chromosome count.

low.restatement: The cell divides twice and ends up with four cells, each holding half the chromosomes.
low.analogy: A library lending half its collection to four branches, no two branches identical.
low.examPointer: The count is four, the content is half, and the products differ.

medium.restatement: Pairing then separation in two rounds guarantees the halving and reshuffles the genetic material.
medium.analogy: Two sorting rounds at a mail depot: first the pairs are split, then the copies.
medium.examPointer: Attach a reason to the halving: fertilisation restores the full set.

check.stem: How many daughter cells does meiosis produce?

options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.
Two is the mitosis count; meiosis divides twice.
No taught stage yields six cells.
Eight would need a third division.

check.stem: What is the chromosome content of each meiotic daughter cell?

options.text: Half the original number, so haploid
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.
That describes mitosis products.
The number halves, it never doubles in the products.
Each daughter keeps one of each pair.

check.stem: What happens during the first meiotic division?

options.text: Chromosome pairs are pulled to opposite ends of the dividing cells
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.
The second division handles the copies.
The first division does real sorting.
Nuclear division is the essence of meiosis.

check.stem: Why are the four products genetically different from one another?

options.text: Each receives a different mix of the starting genetic material
options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.
Cloning describes mitosis, the opposite.
Deletion is not the taught mechanism here.

options.text: Only two of the four differ
options.explanation: All four can differ from one another.

check.stem: Which cells in the body are made by meiosis?

options.text: The gametes, such as sperm, egg, pollen and ovum
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.
Skin renews by mitosis.
They are replaced through mitosis of precursor cells.
Muscle growth uses mitosis, not meiosis.

check.stem: State the two reasons meiosis is important.
check.modelAnswer: It produces the gametes for sexual reproduction and it increases the genetic variation of offspring.

check.stem: Describe how the number of divisions in meiosis compares with mitosis.
check.modelAnswer: Meiosis divides twice, so four haploid cells form, while mitosis divides once and yields two diploid cells.

check.stem: Explain why the chromosome number must halve during gamete formation.
check.modelAnswer: Two gametes fuse at fertilisation, so each must carry half a set; otherwise the zygote would hold double the normal chromosome number every generation.

check.stem: A pollen grain counts 12 chromosomes and the plant's body cells count 24. Which process made the pollen grain, and how many chromosomes did its parent cell start with?
check.modelAnswer: Meiosis made the haploid pollen grain, and its diploid parent cell started from 24 chromosomes before the halving.

lessons.title: Mitosis and Meiosis Side by Side
lessons.opening: The comparison table sets the two divisions side by side, and exams love the differences, so anchor on the ones the table stresses: daughter cell number, chromosome content, genetic identity of products, and the jobs each division does.
keyPoints: Mitosis yields two identical diploid cells; meiosis yields four different haploid cells.
Mitosis drives growth and repair; meiosis builds gametes for reproduction.
Only meiosis runs two divisions; mitosis runs one.
Examiners reward specific differences, so quote numbers and outcomes.

low.restatement: One division clones for maintenance; two divisions halve for reproduction.
low.analogy: A photocopier versus a card dealer: one duplicates exactly, the other deals varied hands.
low.examPointer: Give two or three differences and be specific, as the table demands.

medium.restatement: Number, ploidy and identity move together: two divisions are what allow the halving and the variation.
medium.analogy: Two taps drain a tank lower than one; the extra division is what halves the set.
medium.examPointer: Know the reason behind each difference, not just the difference.

check.stem: Which division produces daughter cells with identical chromosome sets?

options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.
Meiotic products are genetically different.
Only mitosis guarantees identity.
Mitosis is defined by identity.

check.stem: How many divisions does meiosis complete?

options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.
One division is the mitosis pattern.
No third division occurs.
Four counts the products, not the divisions.

check.stem: A question asks for one difference between the two divisions. Which answer scores?

options.text: Mitosis makes two cells, meiosis makes four
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.
Only meiosis makes gametes.
Only meiosis halves; mitosis preserves the set.
Meiosis is central to variation.

check.stem: Which process maintains the chromosome number during ordinary growth?

options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.
Meiosis halves the number for gametes.
Fertilisation restores the number after the halving.
Mutation changes base sequences, not chromosome counts.

check.stem: Why should reasons be attached when naming the division a tissue uses?

options.text: The exam rewards knowing why that division suits the job
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.
The taught hint says reasons matter.
The divisions differ, so the name matters.
Nothing forbids justification; it is demanded.

check.stem: State two differences between mitosis and meiosis.
check.modelAnswer: Mitosis produces two genetically identical diploid cells for growth and repair, while meiosis produces four genetically different haploid gametes.

check.stem: Name the products of each division.
check.modelAnswer: Mitosis gives identical body cells and meiosis gives haploid gametes.

check.stem: Explain why confusing the two divisions loses marks so readily.
check.modelAnswer: Their outputs differ in number, ploidy and genetic identity all at once, so an answer naming the wrong division contradicts every feature the mark scheme checks.

check.stem: A root tip grows longer and a pollen grain forms in the same plant. Match each event to its division and give one reason for each.
check.modelAnswer: Root growth uses mitosis because new identical diploid cells extend the tissue, and pollen formation uses meiosis because gametes must be haploid and genetically different.

glossary.definition: The two-stage division that produces four genetically different haploid cells.
A haploid sex cell produced by meiosis, such as sperm or egg.
Carrying half the normal chromosome number.
Carrying the full double chromosome set.
The single division that produces identical diploid cells.
